A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures, prompts, and annotation interfaces, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original preference-study outcomes, 3,000 newly collected human judgments, 13,600 LLM judgments, and statistical analyses of their responses.

after.justification: v2 retains the original human and LLM experiments, their reported judgments, and the regression and significance-test results.

M1.justification: The GPT-4o rationale-generation workflow, four rationale conditions, and human/LLM rating procedures are unchanged. Appendix A.5 retains the same prompts.

E1.justification: Both evaluate gold and distractor answer plausibility on Social IQA and CommonsenseQA with the same participant population. The newly suggested demographic investigations are future work, not additional evaluations.

E2.justification: The four-model preference comparison in Section 2.1 and the 17 LLM raters in Section 4 retain identical membership. No comparison method is added or removed.

E3.justification: Both retain 100 questions, 200 question-answer pairs, four rationale conditions, five human judgments per added condition, and the same Likert scale and LLM evaluation settings.

E4.justification: The baseline-rating/rationale-type regression, rationale-length regression, and illustrative cases are unchanged. Moving Table 4 into the appendix and discussing its interpretation again do not add an analysis.

E5.justification: Both disclose a single model run in Appendix A.3 and retain the same chi-squared tests, regression t-tests, p-values, and significance markings. No uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: The rating distributions and shifts, regression coefficients, and example outcomes in Tables 2–9 and Figures 1–3 are unchanged. Table 4 retains its values and significance markings after relocation.

T1.justification: No mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised. The new description of the regression as causal is not accompanied by new formal analysis.

C1.justification: The core empirical claims remain intact, but Section 7 expands the claimed implications beyond collaboration and persuasion to human-AI safety, decision support, and commonsense-evaluation methodology.

C2.justification: Sections 3.1 and 6 newly characterize the existing OLS analysis as causal. Section 7 adds future questions about cognitive abilities, age, grade level, and demographics; the existing limitations remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: The appendices retain the same hardware, runtimes, decoding settings, annotation requirements, and prompts. Both versions still promise code and data release upon publication.

R1.justification: The cited works are unchanged. Section 6 adds explicit novelty claims for the opposing effects of PRO rationales on human gold/distractor ratings and for stronger distractor anchoring, sharpening the positioning against prior explanation research.

P1.justification: Changes comprise localized grammar corrections, a new cross-reference to Section 5, an added novelty paragraph in Section 6, and revisions to the conclusion. The broader narrative structure and section order are preserved.

P2.justification: Table 4 moves from the main text on v1 page 8 to the appendix on v2 page 13, above Table 5. Associated reflow moves Prompt A.4 onto page 14; figures, captions, and table designs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added novelty paragraph and concluding question modestly clarify positioning. However, v2 newly labels the unchanged OLS regression causal (Sections 3.1 and 6), without supplying an identification argument for the anchoring mechanism. This stronger interpretation exceeds the added support and slightly reduces scientific caution, outweighing the limited editorial gains.
